description: The East Javan Langur (Trachypithecus auratus), also known as the ebony lutung, Javan langur, or Javan lutung, is an Old World monkey from the Colobinae subfamily. It is found on the Indonesian islands of Java, Bali, and Lombok. Like all colobines, it has evolved a specialized stomach to digest plant material more efficiently, along with enlarged salivary glands to assist in breaking down food. The species is diurnal and arboreal, living in small social groups of around 7 individuals with one or two adult males. Formerly considered to have two subspecies, but the western Javan langur (T. a. mauritius) was elevated to full species status as Trachypithecus mauritius in 2008.
population_estimate: Exact population estimates for the species are not available. Assessed as Vulnerable by IUCN due to population declines from habitat loss and fragmentation across its range on Java, Bali, and Lombok. Java is one of the most densely populated islands in the world, placing enormous pressure on remaining forest habitats. The population trend is decreasing.
habitat: Inhabits the interior and peripheral areas of tropical rainforests on Java, Bali, and Lombok. Found in both primary and secondary forests, as well as deciduous forests, mangrove forests, and plantation areas. Occupies elevations ranging from 255 m to 1,254 m above sea level. They require continuous forest canopy for their arboreal lifestyle and are sensitive to forest fragmentation.
threats: Habitat loss and fragmentation from deforestation on densely populated Java
Hunting and capture for traditional medicine
Small remaining habitat patches limiting population viability
ecosystem_role: As a primarily herbivorous arboreal primate, the East Javan Langur plays an important role in seed dispersal and forest regeneration. Their specialized digestive system allows them to process leaves that many other animals cannot digest, making them effective folivores. They help regulate vegetation growth through their feeding on leaves, fruit, flowers, and flower buds. As a social species, they form an important part of the forest canopy fauna and serve as prey for larger predators such as pythons and birds of prey.
human_connection: The East Javan Langur shares its habitat with over 140 million people on the island of Java — one of the most densely populated islands on Earth. This extreme population pressure has led to severe deforestation and habitat fragmentation. While the species is protected by Indonesian law, enforcement is challenging. The langur's bright orange juveniles have drawn attention, making the species popular in zoos worldwide including Bristol, Twycross, and Bronx zoos. The species serves as an important indicator of forest health on Java.
what_students_can_do: Study how colobine monkeys have evolved specialized digestive systems to process leaves
Learn about Java's remaining protected forests and their importance for biodiversity
Research the impact of human population density on wildlife conservation in Indonesia
Support reforestation and habitat connectivity projects in Java
Document the behavioral ecology of arboreal primates in fragmented forest landscapes
fun_fact: Juvenile East Javan Langurs are born bright orange — this striking coloration may help adults keep track of them and ensure they are always noticed and protected
Their Latin name 'auratus' means 'golden', referring to a rare color morph where adults retain their golden orange juvenile coloration
The tail is nearly twice the length of the body — up to 98 cm compared to a body length of just 55 cm
Like all colobines, they have a specialized, multi-chambered stomach for digesting leaves, similar to ruminants like cows
The species was split in 2008, with the western population now recognized as a separate species called Trachypithecus mauritius
